paper_title: Empowering Edge Agents: A Systematic Analysis of Edge-Cloud Collaboration in LLM Agent Execution

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Edge-cloud collaboration combines the lower inference overhead and greater data locality of edge-side execution with the stronger capabilities of cloud-hosted models. However, as LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon scenarios, cloud participation becomes interleaved throughout execution rather than a one-shot decision for each query. Such interleaved participation introduces trajectory-level effects that remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we introduce EC2-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution. It provides executable digital-workspace agent tasks and a unified evaluation framework covering task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Using this benchmark, we empirically study diverse forms of edge-cloud collaboration. Our study reveals three findings. First, collaboration achieves a favorable balance among task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure compared with edge-only and cloud-only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance, and performance differences across strategies shrink, while privacy exposure remains strongly strategy-dependent. Third, stronger edge capability shifts preferred collaboration from externally controlled cloud participation and direct cloud execution toward more edge-controlled collaboration. Further analyses identify cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction following as important edge-side abilities for effective collaboration. These findings provide a systematic understanding of edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution and insights for designing future edge agents that effectively collaborate with cloud models. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/EC2-Bench.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Edgecloud collaboration offers promising way to combine the lower inference overhead and greater data locality of edge-side execution with the substantially stronger capabilities of cloud-hosted frontier models. However, as LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon scenarios, cloud participation becomes interleaved throughout execution rather than one-shot decision for each query. Such interleaved participation introduces trajectory-level effects that remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we introduce EC2-Bench, benchmark for evaluating edgecloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution. EC2-Bench provides executable digital-workspace agent tasks and unified evaluation framework covering task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Using this benchmark, we empirically study diverse forms of edgecloud collaboration. Our study reveals several key findings. First, edge cloud collaboration provides an effective execution paradigm for long-horizon agents by achieving favorable balance among task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure compared with edge-only and cloud-only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance, and performance differences across collaboration strategies become smaller, while privacy exposure remains strongly dependent on the chosen strategy. Third, stronger edge capability changes the preferred collaboration mode, shifting from externally controlled cloud participation and direct cloud execution toward more edge-controlled collaboration. Further analyses identify cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction following as important edgeside abilities underlying such effective collaboration. These findings establish systematic understanding of edgecloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution and provide insights for designing future edge models that can effectively collaborate with cloud models. All codes and resources are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/EC2-Bench.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) (Achiam et al., 2023), together with the emergence of agent harnesses such as Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025) and OpenClaw (OpenClaw, 2025), have shifted LLM applications from isolated promptresponse interactions toward long-horizon, goal-directed agent execution (Wang et al., 2024a). These agents tackle complex end-to-end workflows, including software development, data analysis, information seeking, and workplace automation, through iterative interaction with external environments and tool use (Yao et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2024b; Shen et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b). Bringing such agents to edge devices, however, remains challenging because edge platforms are inherently constrained by limited computational resources and memory (Qu et al., 2025). Conindicates corresponding author. 1 Arxiv Preprint. sequently, practical on-device deployment often relies on relatively small LLMs (e.g., models with 10B parameters), which can struggle with demanding reasoning, planning, and tool-use tasks (Choi et al., 2026), making reliable long-horizon execution challenging (Liu et al., 2024). To address this limitation, recent work has explored edgecloud LLM collaboration, where lightweight edge models are complemented by cloud-hosted frontier LLMs when additional capability is required (Zhang et al., 2026b). This paradigm combines efficient edge-side execution with stronger cloud capabilities, but requires effective coordination of edge and cloud participation to realize these complementary benefits (Ding et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2024; Agrawal & Mayer). Prior edgecloud LLM systems largely treated collaboration as one-shot coordination process for each query, typically through routing or escalation decisions (Pozi & Sato, 2025; Han et al., 2026). In long-horizon agent execution, however, collaboration can become more interleaved, with edge and cloud models participating at different points along the trajectory as capability requirements change (Yi et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b). Such interleaving introduces trajectory-level dependencies: cloud participation decisions can influence subsequent execution steps, accumulate resource costs over the trajectory, and determine how much potentially sensitive information leaves the local environment. Yet existing analysis still largely focuses on isolated routing or escalation decisions at the query level, leaving these trajectory-level effects underexplored (Hu et al., 2024a; Lu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a; 2025). To close this gap, in this paper, we conduct systematic empirical study of edgecloud collaboration in long-horizon agentic execution. Specifically, we organize our study around three research questions. We first ask: does edgecloud collaboration remain effective for realistic long-horizon agent execution? (RQ1) We evaluate this question jointly in terms of task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. As edge models become more capable, more execution can be handled locally while cloud assistance is reserved for capability-demanding operations. We therefore ask: how does increasing edge capability impact edgecloud collaborative execution? (RQ2); As increasing edge capability changes how computation is distributed between edge and cloud, collaboration strategies that are effective under one capability regime may not remain equally suitable under another. This motivates our final question: how should edgecloud collaboration evolve as edge capability advances? (RQ3). To provide common empirical basis for this study, we introduce EC2-BENCH (EdgeCloud Collaborative Agent Benchmark), an evaluation framework that combines diverse suite of realworld digital-workspace agent tasks with unified execution and evaluation environment for edge cloud collaboration. EC2-BENCH characterizes each configuration along three dimensions: task performance (Yuan et al., 2026b), resource usage (Fang et al., 2025), and privacy exposure. We explicitly consider privacy because cloud participation may reveal sensitive workspace information encountered during agent execution, making privacy exposure an important dimension of evaluating such collaboration (Fu et al., 2026). Using EC2-BENCH, we systematically investigate edgecloud collaboration across diverse agent tasks, collaboration strategies, and edge-capability regimes. Our study yields three main findings. First, edgecloud collaboration remains effective for longhorizon agents: partial cloud participation improves task performance over edge-only execution while requiring substantially less cloud resource usage and privacy exposure than cloud-only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance, and performance differences across collaboration strategies become much smaller; however, their differences in privacy exposure remain substantial. Thus, privacy remains an important differentiator even when task performance converges. Third, the collaboration strategy that works best changes with edge capability. Weaker edge models benefit more from external routing and direct cloud execution, whereas stronger edge models benefit more from edge-controlled invocation and cloud advisory. Further analyses suggest that effective cloud-invocation decisions and instruction following are key edge-side abilities for stronger-edge collaboration modes. These findings highlight the value of optimizing future edge models for both standalone capability and effective cloud collaboration, enabling more capable edge agents.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: A growing body of work has investigated how edge and cloud LLMs can be coordinated to leverage their complementary capabilities and deployment characteristics, balancing overall task performance with local efficiency (Zhu & Yang, 2025; Dong et al., 2025). substantial line of work 2 Arxiv Preprint. focuses on one-shot coordination for individual queries, either by routing each query to an edge or cloud model or by cascading from the local model to the cloud when additional capability is needed (Chen et al., 2023; Ong et al., 2024; Miao & Fang). These approaches therefore center on improving the accuracy of routing and escalation decisions (Ding et al., 2024). More recent work has extended edgecloud collaboration to agent execution, where edge and cloud participation can be coordinated at different steps throughout multi-step trajectory rather than determined once for the entire query, enabling finer-grained use of their complementary capabilities. Within this setting, recent approaches have explored different designs for coordinating edgecloud collaboration, mainly along two dimensions. Some dynamically determine when the cloud model should participate, either through dedicated rule-based controllers or routers, or by allowing the edge agent itself to decide when to invoke the cloud (Shao et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b;a; Zeng et al., 2026b). Beyond deciding when the cloud should participate, other approaches have explored complementary functional roles for edge and cloud models during execution, such as execution, planning, or providing guidance (Yi et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026a). Existing work has begun to develop dedicated evaluation resources for edgecloud LLM systems. LLMSwitchBench (Liu et al., 2025) evaluates edgecloud routing for smart-home queries, while M4A1 (Yuan et al., 2026b) extends devicecloud evaluation to multimodal, multitask, and multiturn conversations, focusing on where individual inference requests should be executed. More general LLM routing benchmarks instead abstract away from the edgecloud setting and evaluate routing systems over heterogeneous model pools, primarily focusing on routing quality and overall costperformance trade-offs (Huang et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026b). Despite this progress, existing evaluations pay more attention on routing decisions for individual queries, tasks, or turns, typically over standalone inference workloads such as knowledge, reasoning, coding, and instruction-following tasks. Our study instead treats edgecloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution as the primary object of empirical analysis, aiming to systematically characterize its effectiveness and system-level behavior across different edge capability levels and collaboration designs.

Query Routing. Query Routing employs an external router to select the model for task before agent execution begins. Routers typically use lightweight scoring or classification model to estimate, from the task instruction ITask, whether the task should be handled by the edge model Me or the stronger cloud model Mc (Ong et al., 2024). The routing decision is made once and remains fixed throughout execution, such that Mt remains either {Me} or {Mc} at every execution step, and the entire trajectory is generated by the selected model. Per-step Routing. Per-step Routing revisits model selection at each interaction step. Instead of making single task-level decision, an external router estimates, based on the task instruction ITask and the partial execution trajectory τ<t, whether the current step can be handled by the edge model Me or should be routed to the stronger cloud model Mc (Zeng et al., 2026c). sections.title: 4 EC2-BENCH: BENCHMARKING EDGE–CLOUD COLLABORATION FOR
sections.content: LONG-HORIZON AGENT EXECUTION To systematically study edgecloud collaboration in agent execution, we introduce EC2-BENCH, comprising 128 executable agent tasks and unified procedure for evaluating different collaboration strategies. For each task, we execute the agent under collaboration strategy and record the resulting collaborative execution trace γC, which captures both the agent trajectory and cloud participation throughout execution. EC2-BENCH then evaluates the resulting execution along three dimensions: task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure, providing comprehensive view of the effectiveness and costs of edgecloud collaboration. These design choices distinguish EC2-BENCH from existing benchmarks for LLM routing and edgecloud collaboration. Table 1 summarizes the key differences among these benchmarks in evaluation scenarios, collaboration modes, and evaluation dimensions, with more detailed comparison provided in Appendix A.2. 4.1 TASK SUITE CONSTRUCTION We construct EC2-BENCH by collecting executable agent tasks from existing benchmarks, curating them for the study of edgecloud collaboration, and augmenting the resulting task suite with sensitivity annotations for privacy-exposure evaluation. Data Collection. We construct the task suite of EC2-BENCH based on six established executable agent benchmarks: Claw-Eval (Ye et al., 2026), WildClawBench (Ding et al., 2026), QwenClawBench (Qwen Team, 2026b), LiveClawBench (Long et al., 2026), PinchBench (PinchBench, 2026), and ClawBench (Zhang et al., 2026c). We select these benchmarks because their tasks evaluate end-to-end agent execution through stateful, multi-step interactions with tools, applications, and workspace artifacts, with explicit task objectives and verifiable execution outcomes. Collectively, they cover broad range of applications, interaction patterns, execution environments, and task difficulties, providing diverse candidate pool for constructing EC2-BENCH. Task Curation. Starting from the collected candidate pool, we further adapt and curate the tasks to construct the final task suite. Specifically, we first adapt tasks from different source benchmarks to common execution environment and evaluation interface, enabling all tasks to be executed under the same agent runtime and evaluated under consistent conditions while preserving their original objectives, workspace states, required interactions, and success criteria. We then apply collaboration-oriented difficulty filtering procedure to retain tasks that are informative for studying 5 Arxiv Preprint. edgecloud collaboration. We evaluate each adapted task under edge-only and cloud-only execution to characterize task difficulty at the two execution endpoints. Tasks that are consistently solved by both endpoints are removed because they provide limited opportunity to differentiate agent execution paradigms, while tasks where neither endpoint achieves meaningful completion are excluded because they provide limited basis for evaluating collaborative execution. Following these steps, we further supplement the task suite with tasks from underrepresented scenarios to maintain broad workload coverage. The resulting task suite consists of 128 executable tasks. To measure the potential exposure of sensitive information from local workspaces to the cloud during collaboration, we further incorporate sensitivity annotations into EC2-BENCH. Specifically, we first annotate sensitive information already contained in the original workspace artifacts. We then use an LLM-based approach to identify appropriate locations, generate realistic synthetic sensitive information, and insert it into relevant workspace artifacts, while preserving the original task objective, required interactions, and evaluation criteria. This process results in fine-grained sensitivity annotations for 100 tasks, where each sensitivity unit corresponds to an atomic piece of sensitive information grounded in workspace artifact. Detailed procedures for task adaptation, collaboration-oriented filtering, coverage supplementation, and sensitivity annotation are provided in Appendix A.3, Appendix A.4 and Appendix A.5. 4.2 EVALUATING COLLABORATIVE EXECUTION Given the collaborative execution trace γC produced by collaboration strategy C, EC2-BENCH evaluates the execution along three dimensions: task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Task performance measures whether the agent accomplishes the task, resource usage quantifies the computation consumed by the edge and cloud models during execution, and privacy exposure measures the fraction of annotated sensitive information units that become visible to the cloud during collaborative execution. Task Performance. We assess task performance using task-specific evaluation checks that cover key requirements for successful completion, including whether the intended outcome is achieved, task constraints are satisfied, and required tool or application interactions are performed correctly. Checks that can be determined directly from task outputs or workspace states are evaluated through rule-based validation or environment-state auditing, while checks requiring semantic judgment are evaluated using rubric-based LLM-as-a-judge (Ding et al., 2026). Given an execution trajectory τ contained in γC, each check produces score in [0, 1], and the task completion score is computed as the weighted average of these check scores according to predefined task-specific weights. Resource Usage. We quantify the resource usage of collaborative execution from both the cloud and edge sides. For the cloud, we record the input, output, and cache-read tokens consumed by all cloud invocations in γC, and compute the corresponding monetary cost according to the pricing of the cloud model. For the edge, we estimate the total floating-point operations (FLOPs) incurred by the edge model throughout the execution trajectory. Privacy Exposure. We measure privacy exposure by quantifying how much sensitive information becomes visible to the cloud during collaborative execution. For each task with sensitivity annotations, let denote its set of sensitivity units. Given the cloud-visible contexts {vc t=1 recorded in γC, we measure privacy exposure as the fraction of sensitivity units disclosed to the cloud: }T Epriv = 1 (cid:88) sS Iexp (cid:0)s, {vc }T t=1 (cid:1) , (5) where Iexp indicates whether the information represented by sensitivity unit is disclosed to the cloud during execution. Since sensitive information may be paraphrased or reformulated rather than reproduced verbatim, we use an LLM-based judge for exposure detection (Zharmagambetov et al., 2026). To validate the automated judge, we compare its predictions against adjudicated human labels on 200 sensitivity unitcontext pairs. The automated judge achieves an F1 score of 96.9% against human annotations, demonstrating high agreement with human judgments and the reliability of our privacy annotations. sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTAL METHODOLOGY
sections.content: This section describes the experimental configurations and evaluation protocol used to study edge cloud collaboration on EC2-BENCH. Execution Configurations. We instantiate the edge side with models of progressively increasing capability from the Qwen series (Qwen Team, 2026a). Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-9B serve as representative edge models under current deployment constraints, while Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.7Plus are included as higher-capability proxies for future edge models. We use GLM-5.3 (Zeng et al., 2026a) as the primary cloud model across all main configurations, given its strong performance on agentic tasks. We further evaluate our findings with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as an alternative cloud model to examine their robustness beyond single cloud model (Appendix A.8). For comparison, we include edge-only and cloud-only execution, where action generation is handled exclusively by Me and Mc, respectively, throughout the task. All configurations are implemented within OpenClaw1, providing shared agent runtime and tool interface across execution settings. Evaluation Protocol. Each taskconfiguration pair is executed independently three times to account for randomness in agent execution (Chan et al., 2025), with results averaged across runs. In addition to the task completion score defined in Section 4.2, we report Pass3 to characterize execution robustness, defined as the fraction of tasks successfully completed in all three runs, where run is considered successful if its completion score exceeds 0.7. Privacy exposure is evaluated on the 100 tasks equipped with sensitivity annotations. For task checks requiring rubric-based semantic judgment and for privacy-exposure detection, we use GPT-5.4-mini (OpenAI, 2026b) with reasoning enabled, following prior practice in LLM-based agent evaluation (Zharmagambetov et al., 2026). Cloud-side monetary cost is computed using OpenRouter2 pricing based on raw input, cache-read input, and output tokens, while edge-side computation is estimated in FLOPs following Kaplan et al. (2020). Detailed pricing assumptions and FLOPs calculations are provided in Appendix A.11.

To probe how collaboration may evolve be8 Arxiv Preprint. yond current lightweight edge models, we additionally include Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.7-Plus as prospective proxies for stronger future edge models. As shown in Table 2, stronger edge models consistently improve collaborative execution and bring its performance closer to cloud-only execution. The best available collaborative configuration increases from 39.97% completion with Qwen3.5-2B to 76.84% with Qwen3.7-Plus, approaching the 82.70% completion of cloud-only execution. We further examine how increasing edge capability changes the variation among collaboration strategies. Specifically, for each edge model, we measure the gap between the highest and lowest completion scores and privacy exposure values. As shown in Figures 3a and 3b, task performance becomes substantially less sensitive to the collaboration strategy as edge capability increases. The completion gap among the evaluated strategies narrows from 25.22% with Qwen3.5-2B to 3.67% with Qwen3.7-Plus. In contrast, privacy exposure does not exhibit the same convergence, with substantial differences persisting across collaboration strategies. Notably, with Qwen3.7-Plus, the strategies differ by only 3.67% in completion but by 66.23% in privacy exposure. These results show that stronger edge capability substantially compresses performance differences across collaboration strategies, while privacy exposure remains highly differentiated. 6.3 HOW DOES EDGECLOUD COLLABORATION EVOLVE WITH EDGE CAPABILITY? (RQ3) Beyond improving collaborative performance, increasing edge capability may also change effective collaboration mechanisms. We examine this shift along two dimensions: who determines cloud participation and what role the cloud plays once invoked. As shown in Table 2, both dimensions exhibit clear shifts with improving edge capability. In terms of participation control, externally routed strategies generally outperform edge-controlled strategies with weaker edge models. For example, with Qwen3.5-2B, Per-step Routing achieves 39.97% completion, compared with 15.86% for EdgeCtrl. Delegation. As edge capability improves, however, this pattern reverses. similar reversal appears in the role of the cloud: weaker edge models benefit more from direct cloud execution, whereas stronger edge models favor advisory support. These shifts motivate further analysis of two edge-side abilities associated with this trend: cloud-assistance decision making and cloud-guidance utilization. Detailed experimental settings and additional analyses are provided in Appendix A.10. (a) Cloud-invocation decision making. Cloud-Assistance Decision Making. The shift toward agent-controlled invocation motivates us to examine whether stronger edge models can make more effective cloud-assistance decisions. Since there is no explicit annotation indicating when cloud assistance is necessary, we compare Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation against matched random-invocation baseline. Specifically, we preserve the same cloud-call rate as the agentcontrolled strategy while randomly selecting invocation steps. As shown in Figure 4a, edge-controlled delegation consistently outperforms random invocation. The gain is only 1.2% for Qwen3.5-2B, but reaches 3.0 4.4% for the more capable edge models. This pattern suggests that stronger edge models may make more effective cloud-invocation decisions. Figure 4: Analysis of edge-side capabilities for increasingly edge-led collaboration. (a) Task completion under agentcontrolled invocation and matched random baseline with the same cloud-call rate. (b) EC2-BENCH task completion of the edge model under cloud advisory during instruction-following training. (b) Guidance following. Cloud Guidance Utilization. We next examine whether instruction-following ability is associated with improved advisory collaboration. Starting from Qwen3.5-2B, we apply targeted instructionfollowing training and evaluate intermediate checkpoints under fixed cloud-advisory setting. As shown in Figure 4b and Appendix A.10, task completion under cloud advisory consistently improves as instruction-following ability develops during training, increasing from 24.8% before training to 28.8% after 600 steps. These results suggest that instruction-following ability is associated with improved utilization of cloud-provided guidance. 9 Arxiv Preprint.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this work, we study edgecloud collaboration for long-horizon LLM agent execution, where cloud participation is interleaved throughout the execution trajectory. To enable systematic investigation of this problem, we introduce EC2-BENCH, an evaluation framework that combines executable digital-workspace agent tasks with unified measurements of task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Our findings show that edgecloud collaboration can achieve favorable balance between capability, cost, and privacy compared with purely edge-side or cloud-side execution. As edge models become stronger, collaborative execution increasingly approaches cloud-only performance, while privacy exposure remains highly dependent on how cloud participation is organized. We further find that stronger edge models benefit from agent-controlled cloud invocation and advisory interaction. Additional analyses suggest that effective cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction-following are important abilities for edgecloud collaboration, motivating future work to develop more capable edge agents by strengthening their ability to collaborate with cloud models.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: Generative AI tools were used to assist with language polishing and improving the clarity of the manuscript. All research ideas, experimental design, implementation, analysis, and conclusions were developed and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the content of the paper.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This work studies edgecloud collaboration for LLM-powered agents and evaluates different collaboration strategies in terms of task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. EC2-BENCH is designed for research evaluation and responsible system development. We do not use real private user data to construct privacy-sensitive benchmark content. When additional sensitive information is required for evaluation, it is synthetically generated and does not correspond to real individuals, organizations, credentials, or financial records. Human annotation is used only to validate benchmark annotations and synthetic content; no annotator personal information is collected or analyzed. The privacy annotations in EC2-BENCH are intended to support systematic evaluation of sensitive information exposed during edgecloud collaboration and to facilitate the development of more privacy-aware agent systems.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: We provide detailed descriptions of the benchmark construction, collaboration strategies, experimental setup, and evaluation procedures in the main paper and appendix. In particular, we document the task adaptation and filtering process, sensitivity annotation procedure and validation, implementations of the four edgecloud collaboration strategies, model and inference configurations, and the metrics used to evaluate task performance, cloud resource usage, edge computation, and privacy exposure. We further report the experimental settings and implementation details for the analyses conducted in each research question. These details are provided to facilitate reproduction of the benchmark and the reported experimental results.

sections.content: A.1 LICENSE All source benchmarks incorporated into EC2-BENCH are used under their respective licenses. Claw-Eval, WildClawBench, QwenClawBench, LiveClawBench, and PinchBench are released under the MIT License, while ClawBench is released under the Apache-2.0 License. We preserve attribution to the original benchmarks for all adapted tasks and follow the redistribution and usage requirements specified by their licenses. A.2 DETAILED COMPARISON WITH PRIOR BENCHMARKS We provide additional details on how EC2-BENCH differs from representative benchmarks for LLM routing and edgecloud collaboration. Overall, prior benchmarks primarily study model allocation over queries or conversational turns and evaluate task quality together with inference-related costs, whereas EC2-BENCH extends the evaluation to long-horizon agent execution, broader collaboration mechanisms, and trajectory-level privacy exposure. We next compare these benchmarks along three aspects: evaluation scenario, collaboration mode, and evaluation dimension. Evaluation Scenario. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate routing over conventional LLM queries or conversational interactions, while EC2-BENCH focuses on long-horizon agent execution in interactive environments. RouterBench (Hu et al., 2024a) evaluates routing across collection of general LLM tasks. LLMRouterBench (Li et al., 2026b) further broadens the task coverage to include software-engineering and tool-use benchmarks in addition to conventional reasoning, knowledge, and code-generation tasks. LLMSwitchBench (Liu et al., 2025) focuses on independent smart-home queries spanning binary, multiple-choice, and open-ended formats. M4A1 (Yuan et al., 2026b) considers multi-modal and multi-task interactions within multi-turn conversations. In comparison, EC2-BENCH evaluates collaboration over multi-step agent trajectories, where models repeatedly interact with tools, applications, and persistent workspace states. Collaboration Modes. Prior benchmarks predominantly study routing-based collaboration, whereas EC2-BENCH additionally considers collaboration in which the edge agent itself controls cloud participation. RouterBench, LLMRouterBench, and LLMSwitchBench formulate model allocation primarily as query routing, where each input query is assigned to selected model. M4A1 allows devicecloud placement to be reconsidered for different tasks throughout multi-turn conversation. EC2-BENCH includes both Query Routing and Per-Step Routing, and further considers two edge-controlled modes. Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation allows the edge agent to decide when to delegate the next execution step to the cloud, while Edge-Controlled Cloud Advisory lets the edge agent request cloud guidance while retaining responsibility for subsequent action generation. Evaluation Dimensions. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate task quality and inference-related efficiency, while EC2-BENCH additionally quantifies privacy exposure over the complete execution trajectory. RouterBench focuses on task performance and economic cost, while LLMRouterBench evaluates performance-oriented and performancecost routing and additionally provides latencyaware analysis. M4A1 jointly considers response quality, latency, and usage cost in devicecloud offloading. LLMSwitchBench incorporates privacy-sensitive queries and privacy-aware routing mechanisms, including local execution and masking before cloud inference, while its main routing evaluation reports task-quality metrics and inference cost. In EC2-BENCH, privacy exposure is directly quantified by tracking which annotated sensitive information from the local workspace becomes visible to the cloud during execution. Resource usage is likewise measured over the complete trajectory, including cloud-side token consumption and monetary cost as well as edge-side computation. A.3 TASK SUITE CONSTRUCTION AND STATISTICS This section provides additional details on the construction and composition of the EC2-BENCH task suite, including collaboration-oriented difficulty filtering, coverage supplementation, and task statistics. 15 Arxiv Preprint. We first collect candidate tasks from multiple Claw-style executable-workspace agent benchmarks and adapt them to the EC2-BENCH execution environment following the protocol in Appendix A.4. We then perform collaboration-oriented difficulty filtering to retain tasks that provide meaningful room for edgecloud collaboration. All filtering runs are conducted on the adapted task instances in the standardized EC2-BENCH environment, using the same workspace states, tool interfaces, and task-specific evaluation checks defined after adaptation. Specifically, each task is evaluated under three endpoint configurations, using Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-9B as representative edge models and GLM-5.3 as the cloud model. We use the resulting task completion scores as the filtering signal to characterize whether task is already handled by edge-only execution, can be completed by cloud-only execution, or remains challenging for both endpoints. We remove tasks that are consistently completed by both edge-only and cloud-only execution, since such tasks provide limited opportunity to differentiate execution paradigms. We also exclude tasks where neither endpoint achieves meaningful completion, since such tasks provide limited basis for evaluating collaborative execution. The resulting task suite focuses on scenarios where edge-only, cloud-only, and collaborative execution can exhibit meaningful differences. Importantly, this criterion does not require all edge models to fail: tasks that are challenging for Qwen3.5-2B but can be handled by Qwen3.5-9B are retained, as they remain informative for studying how collaboration evolves with increasing edge capability. A.5 PRIVACY ANNOTATION This subsection describes how sensitivity-unit annotations are constructed in EC2-BENCH. Since privacy-relevant information in digital workspaces can be distributed across heterogeneous files, application states, and other task artifacts, we adopt an LLM-based annotation process to identify and annotate sensitive information from two sources: information already present in the task environment and realistically synthesized sensitive content introduced into suitable task artifacts. Across the resulting task environments, more than 15,000 information units are represented in total, of which 3,385 are annotated as sensitive, spanning 100 tasks and 12 fine-grained privacy categories. Both 18 Arxiv Preprint. sources are represented under common annotation schema and privacy taxonomy, with annotation quality further validated through human evaluation. The resulting sensitivity-unit annotations are used to measure privacy exposure during collaborative execution. Privacy exposure quantifies the fraction of annotated sensitive information units that become visible to the cloud through cloudvisible contexts along the execution trajectory. Identification of Pre-existing Sensitive Information. For each task, we use an LLM to inspect the local workspace and identify privacy-relevant information. The workspace may contain files, application states, and other task artifacts accessible to the agent during execution. Each identified item is grounded in its source artifact or application record, and the corresponding sensitive content and source location are recorded as sensitivity unit. This grounding establishes both that the information is available within the task environment and where it originates, providing concrete reference for subsequent exposure evaluation. The resulting annotations are stored separately as task metadata. Synthesis of Sensitive Information. To broaden the coverage of sensitivity annotations across tasks and privacy categories, we additionally introduce synthetic sensitive content into suitable task artifacts. We only augment tasks for which such content can be incorporated without changing the task objective, required interaction, expected output, or success criteria. For each eligible task, an LLM-assisted pipeline selects an appropriate artifact and insertion location and generates synthetic sensitive content consistent with the surrounding format and semantics. Each inserted span is then recorded as sensitivity unit using the same annotation schema as pre-existing sensitive information. We further apply separate LLM-based verification step to improve the realism of the synthesized content. The verifier examines whether each synthetic unit resembles plausible real-world sensitive information and replaces unrealistic or placeholder-like values with more realistic synthetic alternatives. A.9 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS This section provides implementation details for reproducing the experiments in EC2-BENCH, including the execution environment and the implementation of the evaluated edgecloud collaboration strategies. Experimental Environment. All experiments are conducted using OpenClaw as the agent execution framework. The maximum context window is configured to 128K tokens, with each individual model interaction limited to 32K tokens. OpenClaw additionally employs an automatic context compression mechanism to manage context growth during long-horizon execution. The agent execution environment is hosted in E2B sandboxes with stable resource allocation to ensure consistent and reliable execution across experiments. All collaboration strategies share the same agent runtime, execution environment, and model deployment configuration. For all experiments, when cloud assistance is requested, vc consists of the current task instruction and the execution history maintained by OpenClaw, including previous actions, tool calls, and environment observations. No additional redaction or privacy filtering is applied before cloud invocation. Query Routing. Query Routing makes single routing decision before agent execution and assigns the entire task trajectory to either the edge model Me or the cloud model Mc. We directly use the matrix-factorization-based router released with RouteLLM (Ong et al., 2024). We calibrate the threshold on the validation set to obtain an approximately 15% cloud-participation rate at the step level and apply the same threshold during evaluation. This target cloud-participation rate is selected 21 Arxiv Preprint. (a) Edge-only performance on EC2-BENCH. (b) IFEval performance. Per-Step Routing. Per-Step Routing revisits the edgecloud decision at every agent interaction step. We adapt the uncertainty signal used by GlimpRouter (Zeng et al., 2026c) to agent execution. Before generating the action at each step, we obtain the edge models next reasoning-token distribution and compute its entropy as an uncertainty score. If the entropy exceeds calibrated threshold, the current step is routed to Mc for action generation; otherwise, generation continues with Me. The routing decision is repeated independently throughout the trajectory. We calibrate the routing threshold on the validation set such that approximately 15% of tasks are assigned to the cloud, aiming to maintain cloud usage level comparable to other collaboration strategies, and apply the same threshold during evaluation. Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation. Unlike the two routing-based strategies above, Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation places the cloud-participation decision within the edge agent itself. The edge model is provided with delegation tool backed by Mc and can invoke it at any point during execution. When invoked, the current conversation history, including previous actions, tool calls, and observations, is forwarded to the cloud model, which directly performs the next agent step. Control then returns to the edge model for subsequent execution. The delegation instruction encourages the edge agent to invoke the cloud before committing to substantive approach, when it encounters difficulty or considers changing its approach, and before declaring the task complete. Thus, both the timing and frequency of cloud participation are determined dynamically by the edge agent rather than by an external router. Edge-Controlled Cloud Advisory. Edge-Controlled Cloud Advisory uses the same agent-controlled invocation mechanism but assigns different role to the cloud model. The edge model is provided with an advisory tool and autonomously decides when cloud guidance is needed during execution. Upon invocation, the current execution history, including previous actions, tool calls, and environment observations, is provided to Mc. The cloud model returns advisory information in natural language, such as plans, suggestions, or corrective feedback. The advice is appended to the edge models context, after which Me generates the next action based on the task instruction, execution history, and received advice.
